catalog_quote: A preliminary account of stress is given in this section. Stress is not lexically contrastive and appears to be weight sensitive. Stress appears on syllables that have a coda. The following examples show stress falling on the heavier syllable, regardless as to whether the heavier syllable is word final or not: "bæR.hu ‘bone’ mE".rEr ‘eel’ ti.je.".jER ‘fantail (bird)’ When all syllables of a root are either light or heavy, stress falls on the penultimate syllable as shown in the following examples: "ku.li ‘dog’ "we.tSe ‘sea almond’ ti."læ.læ: ‘white-eye (bird)’ "lul.fæR ‘owl’ "men.min ‘Malay apple’ "tæl.sil ‘snake’ The analysis of stress in North Ambrym is only preliminary and needs further analysis.

new_statements.translation_language: English (the character " in the examples is the PDF text layer's rendering of the primary-stress mark; R = tap, E = lax e, tS = affricate in the thesis's ASCII-IPA)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word (root) stress is non-contrastive and quantity-sensitive: a closed (heavy) syllable attracts stress wherever it sits in the word, including final position (mE.'rEr 'eel', ti.je.'jER 'fantail'); when the syllables of a root are all light or all heavy, stress defaults to the penultimate syllable ('ku.li 'dog', 'lul.faeR 'owl', 'tael.sil 'snake'). The author explicitly labels the account preliminary.
new_statements.exceptions: None listed beyond the heavy-syllable attraction; one trisyllabic all-light example (ti.'lae.lae: 'white-eye') shows penultimate stress with a long final vowel, not discussed further. Author states the analysis 'is only preliminary and needs further analysis'.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated over roots in citation form (isolated nouns); no discussion of affixed words, phrase-level prominence, or interaction with the vowel-elision rule of section 2.2.4.
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes the Western dialect of North Ambrym (author based in Ranvetlam village, Lolihor/Lonhali district; 'just the Western dialect prevails here', thesis p.39-40); a North-Eastern dialect (Wowan district, Harimal to Konkon) is noted with 'minor phonemic variations'. Fanbyak/Orkon (orko1234, ISO fnb), spoken in an enclave at Ranvetlam, is explicitly treated as a separate language and is NOT covered by this stress statement. Codrington 1885's 'Ambrym' sketch is also North Ambrym (north-west face, Limbol/Loliwara) but is silent on accent.
